171627.meta: 2025 · MAPPA · film · manga by Tatsuki Fujimoto · dir. Tatsuya Yoshihara, script Hiroshi Seko
171627.w: Devils are born from human fears, and the more a thing is feared, the stronger its devil. Denji, a broke teenager fused with his chainsaw-devil dog Pochita, now works as a devil hunter for Public Safety under Makima. In the film he meets Reze, a girl at a café, and falls for her: night swims, a summer-festival date. Ending: Reze is the Bomb Devil hybrid, a Soviet-trained assassin sent for Denji's heart; after the fight she chooses to meet him at the café anyway and is killed by Makima before she arrives.
171627.q: Nothing queer in this arc; it is a straight romance. The queer pieces of Chainsaw Man sit elsewhere in Fujimoto's story: ⚠ Quanxi, the Chinese devil hunter in the next arc, is a lesbian with four fiend girlfriends (manga, not yet animated).
171627.g: Topped the US box office opening weekend at US$17.25M on ~3,000 screens, taking it past US$100M worldwide (ANN, AniTrendz, Oct 2025). In Japan: 6.56M tickets and ¥10.01B by Dec 30, 2025. Critics read the arc as a story about love, betrayal and finding a real connection in a world built on deceit.

9253.meta: 2011 · White Fox · 24 episodes · visual novel by 5pb. / Nitroplus (2009)
9253.w: Akihabara, 2010. Self-styled mad scientist Rintaro Okabe and his "lab members" (Mayuri, hacker Daru, then neuroscientist Kurisu Makise) accidentally build a microwave that sends text messages into the past ("D-mails"). Changing the past shifts the world onto a new "world line," and only Okabe remembers the old ones. SERN, a sinister stand-in for CERN, is hunting time-travel research, and Mayuri dies in every world line Okabe tries. Ending: he undoes every D-mail, has to choose between saving Mayuri and saving Kurisu, and finally reaches the "Steins;Gate" world line where both live.
9253.q: Ruka Urushibara, a shrine maiden assigned male, who says they feel they were meant to be born a girl. Ruka sends a D-mail that changes the past so they are born female, then gives that world up so Okabe can save Mayuri. Official material calls Ruka a cross-dresser motivated by feelings for Okabe; many fans read Ruka as a trans woman. Lists of trans anime characters include Ruka, while articles on the "trap" trope cite Ruka as its textbook example. The show never settles the question, and Ruka giving up the female world line to undo the D-mails is the scene this debate centers on.
9253.g: The visual novel shipped 300,000 copies, and the game series sold over 1 million by 2015. The anime is ranked among the most acclaimed of 2011, especially with Western fans. Its Blu-ray sold 100,000+ copies in the US. Producer Chiyomaru Shikura credits its grounding in real places and real science.

20954.meta: 2016 · Kyoto Animation · film · manga by Yoshitoki Ōima · dir. Naoko Yamada, script Reiko Yoshida
20954.w: A small Japanese town (modelled on Ōgaki, Gifu ⚠). In grade school, Shoya Ishida leads the bullying of Shoko Nishimiya, a deaf transfer student, until the class turns on him and he is left an outcast. Years later, isolated and planning suicide, he learns sign language and seeks her out to make amends, pulling the old classmates back together. Ending: Shoko attempts suicide; Shoya saves her and falls, ends up in a coma, wakes, and the two reconcile. At a school festival he finally looks up at people's faces again.
20954.q: No queer characters or storyline. What it carries is the outsider experience: a kid singled out for being different, a classmate group that punishes difference, self-hatred, and suicide. ⚠ Director Naoko Yamada's next film, Liz and the Blue Bird (2018), is a well-known queer-coded story of two girls.
20954.g: Earned ¥2.3B in Japan (19th of 2016), more than Yamada's own K-On! film, and about US$31–32M worldwide. A rare mainstream anime film on disability, bullying and suicide, with Japanese Sign Language as one of its languages. A thesis notes its many disabled characters, and the English dub cast a deaf actress as Shoko.

156092.meta: 2025 · Chinese donghua (co-produced with Aniplex ⚠) · original · dir. Li Haoling (Link Click, Heaven Official's Blessing)
156092.w: Trust is literal power. Heroes gain abilities in proportion to how much the public believes in them, and the number is measured, displayed on their wrists, and ranked. Every two years the top heroes fight in a tournament that resets the rankings, and "fear value" is the corruption that turns people into villains. Each arc follows one hero's backstory. The first hero, Nice, is really Lin Ling, a PR assistant who packaged ads for ranked heroes and ended up wearing Nice's identity after a deadly accident.
156092.q: The Nice/Wreck relationship is written so close, with a shared bottle of champagne on a couch, that reviewers read it as romantic. Comics Beat's reviewers say the show will never say it outright ("close bros") and tie that to China's restrictions on LGBTQ content in media. Li Haoling's earlier Heaven Official's Blessing adapted a Chinese BL novel. Queer content that gets through censorship only as subtext is the thing to look at here.
156092.g: Called one of the most underrated anime of 2025. A Chinese-made series with a Japanese voice cast (Natsuki Hanae as Nice) is a co-production model that is new for the industry. It also works as a satire of celebrity, PR and public opinion.

20665.meta: 2014–15 · A-1 Pictures · 22 episodes + OVA (Noitamina) · manga by Naoshi Arakawa
20665.w: Kōsei Arima was a child piano prodigy drilled by his sick mother. After she died he stopped being able to hear his own playing. At 14 he meets Kaori Miyazono, a free-spirited violinist who drags him back onto the stage, with childhood friends Tsubaki and Watari around them. Ending: Kaori, secretly terminally ill, dies during surgery while Kōsei plays in a competition. Her letter reveals the "lie": she pretended to like Watari only so she could get close to Kōsei. Tsubaki admits she has loved Kōsei all along.
20665.q: No queer characters or storyline; every romance in it is straight. Anime Feminist criticizes Kaori as "an obvious device, perfectly constructed to heal Kousei's psychological wounds" (the manic-pixie-dream-girl trope).
20665.g: Won the 37th Kodansha Manga Award (Best Shōnen, 2013), and the manga had 5M+ copies in print by 2017. The anime was widely praised for its animation, soundtrack and performances of real classical pieces. It's a standard pick for "anime that makes you cry," about grief, a parent's abuse, and art as a way back to feeling.

150672.meta: 2023– · Doga Kobo · TV · manga by Aka Akasaka (story) and Mengo Yokoyari (art)
150672.w: Rural doctor Gorō's favorite idol, 16-year-old Ai Hoshino, turns up at his hospital secretly pregnant. A stalker kills him, and he is reborn as her son Aquamarine, with his late patient Sarina reborn as Ai's daughter Ruby, both keeping their memories. Ai is stabbed to death at her door by an obsessed fan. Aqua goes into show business (a reality-dating show, stage plays) to find his biological father, the man behind her murder, while Ruby chases idol stardom. The show covers idol "no dating" rules, manufactured reality TV, and online harassment: Akane is driven to a suicide attempt by a pile-on over a reality show.
150672.q: No canon queer characters. Its subject is people forced to hide who they are behind a performed image: Ai hides her children, and her "I love you" to fans is a lie she hopes will come true. It's a story about the cost of a public persona and the closet that the industry demands.
150672.g: Its opening song, YOASOBI's "Idol," was the first Japanese-language song to top Billboard's Global Excl. US chart (June 2023). The 90-minute first episode became an event. Critics read it as showing the industry's abuses as built into how the industry works, not exceptions to it.

101759.meta: 2019 (S1), 2021 (S2) · CloverWorks · TV · manga by Kaiu Shirai (story) and Posuka Demizu (art)
101759.w: Grace Field House looks like an idyllic orphanage run by "Mom," Isabella, for orphans with numbers tattooed on their necks. At 11, Emma, Norman and Ray learn that the children are livestock, raised to feed demons, and that Isabella is a former orphan who became their keeper. They plan an escape with the whole house. Ending (S1): Norman is shipped out, Ray fakes his own death, and Emma leads the older children over the wall. Season 2 cuts most of the manga and rushes to an ending where the children return to the human world.
101759.q: No canon queer characters. Editor Suguru Sugita first proposed making Emma a boy to suit a shōnen magazine, and the lead stayed a girl. Isabella is a woman forced into a mother role that the system designed for her. ⚠ Norman/Ray is a popular fan pairing.
101759.g: The manga won the 63rd Shogakukan Manga Award (shōnen) and topped Kono Manga ga Sugoi! 2018 for male readers. Season 1 is considered one of the best anime of the 2010s; Season 2 was panned for cutting the manga's story.

20464.meta: 2014–2020, films 2024–25 · Production I.G · 4 seasons + films · manga by Haruichi Furudate (2012–2020)
20464.w: Short Shōyō Hinata is obsessed with volleyball after watching the "Little Giant" play for Karasuno High. At Karasuno he's forced to team up with Tobio Kageyama, the "King of the Court," a genius setter whose old team abandoned him. Their freak quick attack revives a fallen team. The story is the run to Nationals and the rival schools (Aoba Johsai, Nekoma, Shiratorizawa, Inarizaki). Ending (manga): a time-skip to the pros, with Hinata and Kageyama facing each other in the Olympics.
20464.q: No characters are labelled gay or bi. It has one of the biggest queer fandoms in anime, built on its intense bonds between boys: Hinata/Kageyama, Nishinoya/Asahi, and others. A podcast, Fly: A Queer Haikyuu Podcast, reads the series through a queer lens. Fans argue about whether reading it this way is legitimate or "just fujoshi," and that argument is the point to look at here.
20464.g: Haikyu!! The Dumpster Battle (2024) opened to ¥890M on day one, passed ¥10B in Japan and about US$100M worldwide. Four seasons, four films and five OVAs. It's widely called the defining modern sports anime.

9756.meta: 2011 · Shaft · 12 episodes + films (Rebellion, 2013) · original, written by Gen Urobuchi, dir. Akiyuki Shinbo
9756.w: Kyubey, a cute white creature, offers girls one wish in exchange for becoming magical girls who fight witches. Middle-schooler Madoka watches her friends Sayaka, Mami and Kyoko fight and die, while the transfer student Homura works to stop her from signing. The truth: the contract puts the girl's soul in a gem, a magical girl who despairs becomes a witch, and Kyubey's species harvests that energy. Homura is a time-traveller who has relived the same month over and over trying to save Madoka. Ending: Madoka wishes away every witch before it is born and becomes a godlike Law of Cycles, remembered only by Homura. In Rebellion, Homura tears that god apart to bring Madoka back, saying it's because of love, and becomes a demon.
9756.q: Homura's devotion to Madoka is the core of the story, and yuri sites (Okazu, Yuricon) treat it as the central relationship. Homura's Rebellion line that she did it out of love is taken by many as proof it was never just subtext. Others say it is still subtext, and Okazu says the English dub makes it "practically gone." A 2025 critique says Rebellion treats queer love as something that corrupts.
9756.g: Won the 15th Japan Media Arts Festival Animation Grand Prize. The jury praised it as an original work that undermined the assumptions of the magical-girl genre. It also won the 2012 Tokyo Anime Award (Television), the Seiun Award, the Animation Kobe Award and 12 Newtype awards. It's the standard example of a "dark magical girl" deconstruction.

116589.meta: 2021–22 · A-1 Pictures · 23 episodes · light novel by Asato Asato
116589.w: The Republic of San Magnolia says its war with the Giad Empire's drone army, the Legion, is fought with no human casualties. In truth the drones are piloted by the "86": the country's colored minorities, stripped of citizenship, declared non-human and locked in the 86th Sector. Vladilena "Lena" Milizé, a privileged Alba officer, commands the Spearhead squadron by radio without ever seeing them, while its captain Shin, the "Reaper," hears the voices of the dead inside the Legion. Ending (S1): the squadron is sent on a suicide march; part 2 picks them up in the Federacy of Giad, and Lena and Shin finally meet.
116589.q: No canon queer characters; the romances are Lena/Shin, Anju/Daiya and Kurena's crush on Shin. What it gives queer viewers is its subject: a state that legally redefines a group of people as non-human, and a privileged person learning what that system costs.
116589.g: Critics call it one of the best war anime, an anti-war and anti-racism story read as an allegory of segregation and the Holocaust that also questions the white-savior trope. Slashfilm notes it is a rare war story by a woman. The novel won the 2016 Dengeki Novel Prize Grand Prize.

101922.meta: 2019 · ufotable · TV, 26 episodes (season 1) · manga by Koyoharu Gotouge (2016–2020, 23 volumes)
101922.w: Taishō-era Japan (early 1900s). Demons, all made by the original demon Muzan Kibutsuji, eat people at night, and only sunlight or a beheading with a special sword kills them. A secret Demon Slayer Corps hunts them, led by its strongest swordsmen, the Hashira. Tanjiro Kamado, a kind charcoal-seller's son, comes home to find his family slaughtered. His sister Nezuko survives as a demon who refuses to eat humans, and he trains, joins the Corps, and carries her on missions in a box on his back. He picks up two companions: Zenitsu, a coward who fights well only when unconscious, and Inosuke, a boar-masked boy raised wild. Season 1 runs through Asakusa (where he meets the demon doctor Tamayo), the Drum House and Mount Natagumo. There the demon Rui forces other demons into a fake "family," and Tanjiro beats him by remembering his father's Hinokami Kagura dance. Ending: the Hashira spare the siblings, and the trio board a train with the Flame Hashira Rengoku, which leads straight into the Mugen Train film. The manga's full story ends with Muzan held until sunrise, Nezuko human again, and an epilogue of their descendants in a demon-free modern Japan.
101922.q: Nothing in it is explicitly queer, and no reputable source frames it that way. Its angle is masculinity. Tanjiro is a male action lead whose strength is open emotion: he cries, grieves for the demons he kills, and is gentle with allies. Anime Feminist (Amaya Baptiste, 2023) argues that sets him apart in a genre that treats feelings as "uncool," and the online fights over calling him a "crybaby" show it's still contested. The Rui arc sets a family forced on its members against a bond the members chose and keep. ⚠ Fans often cite Mitsuri Kanroji, a later Hashira, as a woman pushing back on gender expectations; not confirmed in a reliable source, and she barely appears in season 1.
101922.g: The Mugen Train film (2020) became the highest-grossing anime and Japanese film of all time. The manga was Oricon's best-seller of 2019 and 2020, has 220M+ copies in circulation, and is credited with keeping Japanese print sales nearly flat during COVID. It won a Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize Special Prize and the Japan Cartoonists Association Grand Prize (2021). ⚠ Episode 19 ("Hinokami") is widely remembered as a landmark of TV animation.

128546.meta: 2021 · WIT Studio · TV, 13 episodes · original anime by Tappei Nagatsuki (Re:Zero) and Eiji Umehara
128546.w: A near future where every AI is built for a single life mission. Diva, the first autonomous humanoid AI, sings at the theme park NiaLand, and her mission is "to make everyone happy with my singing." Matsumoto, an AI from 100 years ahead in a teddy-bear-shaped body, takes over her systems. He warns that AIs will wage a war of extinction against humans and recruits her, as "Vivy," to change history at key "singularity points" decades apart. She tries to save a politician who backs the AI Naming Law, a law giving AIs some rights, and fails to save her young fan Momoka. She stops the space hotel Sunrise from falling, and the AI twin sisters Estella and Elizabeth die saving its passengers. She shuts down Metal Float, an AI factory island whose core is Grace, an AI married to the human Dr. Saeki, in the original history the first human-AI couple. She loses her memories and gets them back in a long conflict with Yugo Kakitani of the anti-AI group Toak. Running through all of it is Vivy's struggle to write a song of her own, something no AI has done. Ending: the shared AI network Archive starts the uprising anyway. Sent back in time, Vivy sings her own song from the NiaLand stage; it works as a shutdown program, Matsumoto sacrifices himself, and the AIs stop at the cost of Vivy herself. A post-credits scene shows her rebuilt without her memories.
128546.q: ⚠ No source found reads the show as queer, and nothing in it is explicitly LGBTQ+. The plot turns on whether a class of beings gets names, rights and legal recognition. Anime Feminist's first-episode review flagged that as the hinge: done badly it becomes "if you give someone basic rights, they'll rise up and destroy the world," done well it's real commentary. Grace and Saeki's marriage is one society treats as unprecedented, the first human-AI couple. The twins Estella and Elizabeth are an intense two-person bond that ends in a final duet. The core question is whether you are the role you were built for or who you choose to become.
128546.g: An original story, voted Best New Anime of Spring 2021 in Anime Corner's poll. Praised for WIT Studio's action and for its music, where songs are plot events. Reviews single out an AI writing its own song as its mark of personhood. Anime News Network felt the post-credits scene undercut the finale.

101291.meta: 2018– · CloverWorks · TV, 13 episodes (2018), films 2019 and 2023, season 2 (2025), final film Oct 2026 · light novels by Hajime Kamoshida
101291.w: Present-day Fujisawa, by the sea. Teenagers are hit by "Adolescence Syndrome," strange events driven by teenage anxiety and social pressure, which turn each girl's inner problem into a literal sci-fi effect. Sakuta Azusagawa is a sardonic high-schooler with a bad reputation and unexplained scars on his chest, and his friend Rio Futaba supplies quantum-physics explanations for each case. Mai Sakurajima, a famous actress on hiatus, stops being noticed by anyone but him; he brings her back by shouting a public confession of love, and they become a couple. Tomoe Koga's wish to keep a fake relationship going traps everyone in a time loop. Rio's insecurities split her into two people. Mai's half-sister Nodoka swaps bodies with Mai out of an inferiority complex. Sakuta's sister Kaede was badly cyberbullied, can't leave the house, and has lost her memory and personality. Ending: Kaede's original self comes back and the gentle personality of the past two years is gone, and Sakuta grieves her as a lost sister. He is comforted by Shoko Makinohara, his first crush, whose return sets up the film Dreaming Girl, where a time paradox threatens Mai's life and Sakuta and Shoko change the past so they never meet.
101291.q: ⚠ No queer reading found in a source, and no main character is canonically LGBTQ+. Its central image is Mai erased because people stop seeing her. It treats identity problems as real and not the sufferer's fault: dissociation, a split self, wanting to be someone else, cyberbullying. Sakuta's rule is that the cure is someone who sees you and believes you.
101291.g: Known for taking a premise that sounds like fanservice (the "bunny girl" title) and delivering a sincere drama about mental health: cyberbullying, self-harm stigma and dissociation, inside a romance between equals. The SF Encyclopedia names kindness as its main theme. ⚠ A Crunchyroll Anime Award is suggested but not confirmed.

124080.meta: 2021 · CloverWorks · TV, 13 episodes (+ The Missing Pieces, 2023) · manga by HERO and Daisuke Hagiwara (2011–2021, 16 volumes), from HERO's webcomic
124080.w: An ordinary Japanese high school, no fantasy. Kyoko Hori is popular and polished at school, but at home she's a blunt homebody who does the housework and raises her little brother Souta while their parents work. Izumi Miyamura looks gloomy and nerdy at school, but outside he's gentle and good with kids, with long hair hiding nine piercings and long sleeves hiding his tattoos. They discover each other's other selves and fall in love; they're a couple by episode 5. The show follows their friend group (Ishikawa, Yoshikawa, Sengoku, Remi, the transfer student Yanagi) and Miyamura facing his middle-school past, when he was shunned and framed by a bully. ⚠ Fans read his self-done piercings as a sign of past depression or self-harm; implied, never stated. Ending: at graduation Miyamura vows he "won't look away from what he used to be anymore" and leaves with Hori.
124080.q: ⚠ No source treats it as an LGBTQ+ work, and the main couples are straight. It plays with gender roles: Hori is the short-tempered, dominant one who plays the mother at home, and Miyamura is the soft, domestic, androgynous-looking boy. Its central idea is the hidden second self, the one that's safe at home versus the one shown at school, and the relief of one person seeing both. In The Missing Pieces episode 8, Yanagi is shown as attractive to "everyone, man or woman." One reader review faults its gender stereotypes, so the angle is debated.
124080.g: One of the best-loved rom-coms of the 2020s, praised because the couple gets together early, so the story is about being in a relationship, not a will-they-won't-they. It treats loneliness, bullying and self-image gently. The manga ranked sixth in the 2014 Nationwide Bookstore Employees' Recommended Comics, and a live-action film and drama followed in 2021.

114535.meta: 2021 · Brain's Base · TV, 20 episodes (seasons 2–3 by Drive, 62 episodes in all) · manga by Yoshitoki Ōima (A Silent Voice), 2016–2025, 25 volumes
114535.w: A pre-modern, folkloric world. A figure called the Beholder casts an immortal orb onto Earth that can take the form of anything that leaves a strong impression on it, and comes back after death. It becomes a rock, then a dying wolf, then an abandoned boy whose tribe left for a "paradise" and who dies alone in the snow. In the boy's form it becomes Fushi and learns to be a person from the people it meets: March, a girl chosen as a sacrifice, who names and mothers him; her friend Parona; the old woman Pioran, who teaches him to speak; Gugu, a masked boy he lives with for years; and Tonari, a girl on the prison island Jananda. Each death adds a body to Fushi's set, including girls' and women's bodies, while enemies called Nokkers try to steal those forms and memories. Hayase, a warrior obsessed with Fushi, kills Parona and impersonates her, tries to sexually assault him, and declares her love. Ending: Pioran, dying, asks to be reborn as something useful to Fushi. A time jump shows him still fighting Nokkers decades later, while Hayase starts a lineage that will keep hunting him. The manga ends in the present day, with Fushi turning down godlike power to become the world's guardian.
114535.q: Fushi has no fixed sex or gender. He wears male and female bodies as he needs them, March's and Parona's included, so identity is shown as built from relationships, not from the body. Anime News Network's reviewer wrote about struggling over Fushi's pronouns and kept "he" because Fushi identifies most with the boy's form, and one character database lists Fushi as genderfluid. In manga volume 8 (past season 1), a friend tells Fushi that "men can love men," and a man's love for another man is shown sympathetically. AIPT called that progressive, then criticized a later twist and "I'm not 'that way'" lines for steering away from it.
114535.g: A slow, grief-heavy story about becoming human through loss: every bond Fushi forms ends, and he carries each person forward as a form. The manga won Best Shōnen at the 43rd Kodansha Manga Awards (2019). The anime won Best Drama at the 6th Crunchyroll Anime Awards (2022) and was nominated for an International Emmy (Kids: Animation). The March and Gugu arcs are the most praised.

143270.meta: 2022 · A-1 Pictures · TV, 13 episodes · original anime (story by Asaura, dir. Shingo Adachi, characters by Imigimuru)
143270.w: Modern Tokyo looks almost free of crime. That is a cover story kept up by the DA (Direct Attack), a secret agency whose killers, the Lycoris, are orphan girls in schoolgirl uniforms who wipe out threats before anyone hears about them. Takina Inoue is sent away from DA headquarters after disobeying orders to save a fellow agent. She lands at LycoReco, a Japanese-style café that takes DA jobs on the side, run by Mika (Chisato's former handler and father figure) with Mizuki and the hacker Kurumi. There Takina is paired with Chisato Nishikigi, the strongest Lycoris, who refuses to kill and uses non-lethal rounds. Chisato lives on an artificial heart from the Alan Institute, whose Yoshimatsu wants her to repay it by becoming a killer, while the terrorist Majima, a former Alan child, tries to expose the Lycoris. Ending: Yoshimatsu sabotages Chisato's heart, and the only replacement is the artificial one in his own chest. Mika shoots him to save her, so Chisato survives the fight with Majima. She throws away her Alan necklace and runs off to Hawaii, where Takina tracks her down and tells her the new heart came from Yoshimatsu. ⚠ How the café crew ends up in the Hawaii epilogue is not confirmed.
143270.q: Mika and Yoshimatsu are confirmed as former partners in a same-sex relationship who together raised and trained Chisato as their surrogate daughter, so her backstory is one of two queer fathers, and their story ends in tragedy in the finale. Chisato and Takina are the show's emotional center. Reviewers call them queer-coded or "semi-canon," but the show never makes it explicitly romantic (no kiss, no confession). Yuri readers took the series up widely, and yuri critic Erica Friedman reviewed it (7/10).
143270.g: An original story, not an adaptation, and the surprise hit of 2022. Its first Blu-ray volume was Japan's best-selling TV-anime disc of the year, and it won Best Original Anime at the 7th Crunchyroll Anime Awards. Critics praised its characters, action and acting. Anime News Network and Anime Feminist criticized its tonal swings and how it treats state violence. At its center is an assassin who won't kill.

142770.meta: 2022 · CoMix Wave Films · film, 121 min · original, written and directed by Makoto Shinkai
142770.w: Present-day Japan, where abandoned places hold doors that open onto the Ever-After, a realm of the dead. Behind them lives a giant "worm" that causes earthquakes if it gets out, and "closers" like Souta Munakata travel the country locking those doors. Suzume Iwato, 17, lives in Kyushu with her aunt Tamaki, who raised her after Suzume's mother died in the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami. Suzume opens a door in a ruined hot-spring resort and pulls out a keystone, which turns into Daijin, a talking cat. Daijin curses Souta into a child's three-legged chair, and the three chase each other across Japan closing doors, until Souta himself becomes the keystone. Ending: Suzume returns to her childhood home in Tōhoku and finds the door she wandered through as a little girl. Inside the Ever-After she frees Souta, Daijin goes back to being a keystone, and she gives her four-year-old self the chair her mother built. A year later she meets Souta again on the road where they first met.
142770.q: Not in the finished film. Shinkai has said he first pitched Suzume as a love story between two girls, a "sisterhood type of romantic story." A producer told him the Japanese market was "too early" for that and pushed him toward a boy-meets-girl romance like Your Name. He made the male lead a chair partly so it wouldn't become too much of a romance. Autostraddle and Gaysi covered it as "almost a lesbian love story." It is an on-record case of a queer romance being turned down for a big-budget film.
142770.g: Shinkai's most direct work about the 2011 disaster, which he said he wanted to show head-on for young people who don't remember it. It grossed about US$315M worldwide, competed for the Golden Bear at the 73rd Berlin Film Festival, and earned a Golden Globe nomination and seven Annie nominations. It won Best Film at the Crunchyroll Anime Awards.

151807.meta: 2024 · A-1 Pictures · TV, 12 episodes (season 2 Jan–Mar 2025) · Korean web novel by Chugong (2016), webtoon drawn by DUBU (Redice Studio)
151807.w: Present-day Korea, years after Gates (portals into monster-filled dungeons) began opening around the world. Some people woke up with powers and became Hunters, ranked E to S, and clearing dungeons is now a dangerous industry. Sung Jin-woo is "the world's weakest hunter," an E-rank who takes raid work to pay for his comatose mother's hospital care ⚠ and to support his younger sister. A hidden "double dungeon" nearly kills him, and he wakes up with the System, a game-like interface only he can see that lets him level up, something no other Hunter can do. Ending: in the season 1 finale ("Arise") he clears his job-change quest, becomes the Shadow Monarch, and raises the knight commander Igris as his first shadow soldier.
151807.q: ⚠ No LGBTQ+ characters, storylines or themes found in season 1, and no critic arguing for one. Its canon romance is Jin-woo and Cha Hae-in. ⚠ A fan pairing of Jin-woo and his sidekick Yoo Jin-ho exists, with only a weak source.
151807.g: The biggest crossover so far of Korean web fiction into anime. The webtoon has 650M+ cumulative readers on Piccoma. The anime won seven awards at the 9th Crunchyroll Anime Awards (2025), including Anime of the Year, Best New Series, Best Action, Best Main Character and Best Score (Hiroyuki Sawano).

132405.meta: 2022 · CloverWorks · TV, 12 episodes (season 2 Jul–Sep 2025) · manga by Shinichi Fukuda (2018–2025, 15 volumes)
132405.w: A present-day Japanese high school and its cosplay scene. Wakana Gojo, raised by his grandfather, a hina-doll craftsman, wants to be a doll-head artisan. He hides it because a childhood friend mocked him as a boy for liking "girls' dolls." Marin Kitagawa, the most popular girl in class, catches him sewing and turns out to be a hardcore otaku who wants to cosplay but can't sew. He makes her costumes, using his skills in fabric, wigs and makeup. They are joined by the perfectionist cosplayer Juju Inui and her very tall younger sister Shinju, who wants to cosplay a male character. Ending: Marin's festival plans fall through, but they reach the fireworks anyway and he carries her home. On a late-night phone call he falls asleep, and Marin confesses her love while he is unaware.
132405.q: The premise is built on breaking gender norms. A boy whose craft is called "feminine" isn't shamed by the story; his skill drives it. Anime Feminist (Archie Fenn) writes that the show treats cosplay as a way to express gender, and Shinju's wish to cosplay a male character is met with understanding, not ridicule. The same essay credits Gojo with refusing to sexualize the girls, while noting that the camera still lingers on Marin. Season 2 (2025) adds Amane Himeno, a male university student who cosplays female characters, and treats his craft seriously. No character in season 1 is stated to be LGBTQ+.
132405.g: One of the best-loved romcoms of the 2020s, with 15M+ manga copies in circulation. Much of its warmth comes from showing how cosplay is actually made (fabric, wigs, contacts, makeup, photo shoots) and from two otaku who take each other's passions seriously. It was adapted as a live-action drama in 2024.

128893.meta: 2023 · MAPPA · TV, 13 episodes (season 2 Jan–Mar 2026) · manga by Yuji Kaku (2018–2021, 13 volumes)
128893.w: Late Edo-period Japan. The shogun sends death-row convicts to Shinsenkyo, an island said to be paradise and to hold the Elixir of Life, and promises a full pardon to whoever brings it back. Each convict is shadowed by a Yamada Asaemon executioner. Gabimaru "the Hollow," a ninja who can't be executed, goes in order to get back to his wife, with Sagiri as his executioner, a woman in a clan of male executioners. The island is ruled by the Tensen, seven near-immortal hermits who use Tao (life energy split into yin and yang) to shift between male and female bodies. Ending (S1): Shion destroys the Tensen Mu Dan with help from Sagiri and Nurugai, after many Asaemon have died. Gabimaru has burned through so much Tao that he has lost his memories, and the season ends with him trying to recall his past.
128893.q: The villains are beings whose sex is fluid. Each Tensen moves between a yin (female) and a yang (male) body at will, and the anime gives each one two voice actors, one male and one female. Mei is the exception, made only yin and unable to switch, and she was used as a yin "partner" against her will. Sagiri's arc is about being a woman in a role reserved for men. ⚠ No critic found who frames the Tensen as LGBTQ+ representation.
128893.g: Crunchyroll grouped it with Jujutsu Kaisen and Chainsaw Man as Shōnen Jump's "Dark Trio," and the manga passed 6.5M copies by 2024. Under the gore, the question is what makes a life worth living: a killer who believes he is hollow keeps going for love of his wife.

19603.meta: 2014–15 · ufotable · TV, 13 + 13 episodes · the "Unlimited Blade Works" route of the 2004 visual novel by Kinoko Nasu / TYPE-MOON
19603.w: Fuyuki City hosts the Holy Grail War, a secret ritual held every few generations. Seven mages ("Masters") each summon a "Servant," the spirit of a legendary hero in one of seven classes, and they fight until one pair is left to claim a Grail that supposedly grants any wish. Rin Tohsaka, heir to an old mage family, enters with her Servant Archer. Her classmate Shirou Emiya, an amateur mage who wants to be a "hero of justice" like his adoptive father Kiritsugu, gets dragged in, is fatally wounded, survives because Rin saves him, and summons Saber by accident. Rin and Shirou become wary allies, and Archer openly despises Shirou. The core twist is that Archer is a future version of Shirou who has come to hate the ideal Shirou lives by. Ending: Archer betrays Rin and fights Shirou over whether that ideal is worth holding, and Shirou refuses to give it up. Archer then sacrifices himself against Gilgamesh, Saber destroys the corrupted Grail, and Shirou and Rin leave for London to study magic.
19603.q: ⚠ No source found that discusses LGBTQ+ content in it, and Wikipedia's article and episode list mention none. The measurable queer angle is fan shipping of Shirou and Archer: Archive of Our Own lists 58 works under that pairing.
19603.g: One of the best-known anime adaptations of a visual novel, and critics singled out ufotable's animation, one reviewer calling it among the most beautiful TV anime they had seen. It topped Japanese home-video charts and won several Newtype awards, including Best Work, Best Director (Takahiro Miura) and Best Theme Song ("Brave Shine"). The whole plot argues one question: is a self-sacrificing ideal worth holding when its endpoint is a burned-out version of yourself?

853.meta: 2006 · Bones · TV, 26 episodes · manga by Bisco Hatori (2002–2010, 18 volumes)
853.w: Ouran Academy is a school for the very rich. Haruhi Fujioka, a scholarship student with short hair and hand-me-down clothes, walks into the Host Club, where six rich boys entertain female students over tea, and knocks over an 8-million-yen vase. The members take her for a boy, so she works off the debt as a host; her blunt, practical manner makes her popular, and the hosts keep her secret. The club is led by Tamaki Suoh, a dramatic half-French romantic, with the calculating Kyoya, the twins Hikaru and Kaoru (who perform a "brotherly love" act for customers), Honey and Mori. At home, Haruhi lives with her father Ranka, who works at a drag/okama bar. It's mostly episodic comedy parodying shōjo romance tropes. Ending: Tamaki's grandmother arranges his engagement to the French heiress Éclair and the club is to be dissolved. Haruhi chases the carriage, falls from a bridge, and Tamaki jumps after her; she persuades him to stay, the club survives, and the anime closes with a dance at the Ouran Fair, the romance left open. ⚠ Carriage details from fan wiki and recap sites.
853.q: Many viewers who grew up in the mid-2000s count it as one of the first places they saw queer people living openly on screen. Kat Schmidt (Anime Herald) calls Haruhi "as gender apathetic as they come," reads her as pansexual and demiromantic, and suggests a modern version might make her non-binary. Ranka is canonically bisexual and a drag performer, shown mostly warmly. The hosts' gay-flavored performance, including the twins' act, parodies how girls' romance media sells boy-boy intimacy, and ANN's Rose Bridges calls it the first "fujoshi comedy." Scholar Tania Darlington ties it to shōjo manga's long history of gender-fluid stories. The criticism is real too: the English dub calls Ranka a slur (Japanese "okama"), the Zuka Club fits the "predatory lesbian" stereotype, characters push Haruhi to act more feminine, and a Bitch Flicks essay argues it ends up reinforcing the gender binary. Hatori said Haruhi's cross-dressing is just the clothes she likes, "without subtext."
853.g: A defining 2000s shōjo comedy and a gateway anime for a generation, praised for skewering romance and otaku clichés rather than just using them. The manga had 14M+ copies in circulation by January 2026, and the series spawned a live-action drama and film, a visual novel and stage musicals.

155907.meta: 2023 · P.A. Works · TV, 12 episodes · original anime, story by Vio Shimokura
155907.w: Present-day Tokyo's world of contract killers. Kazuki Kurusu is an outgoing fixer who gambles and chases women; Rei Suwa is a quiet assassin raised from childhood by his father's organization to kill, who spends his time off on video games. The two live together. On Christmas, during a hotel hit, four-year-old Miri wanders into the gunfight looking for her father, a mob boss, and the target they kill turns out to be him. Kazuki claims to be her dad, and the two men end up raising her while still taking jobs: daycare, money, bedtime, and the search for Miri's mother, Misaki. Miri calls them both "Papa," and Rei slowly accepts that he is one of her fathers. Ending: Misaki returns, dying of throat cancer, and Miri goes to live with her before Misaki is killed by the antagonist Ogino. Kazuki and Rei quit killing, and Rei cripples his own arm to break from his family's organization. A time skip shows the two men running a diner together with a teenage Miri.
155907.q: The show never makes Kazuki and Rei a romantic couple, but it's widely read as a queer family story: two men who choose each other and co-parent outside the nuclear family. In AnimeFeminist, Michele Kirichanskaya reads their bond as a queerplatonic relationship, a committed partnership that from outside "looks indistinguishable from romance" (Julie Sondra Decker), and notes the men split childcare and housework evenly. She criticizes the show for killing off Miri's mother. ⚠ A claim that the director hoped viewers would wonder whether the two are a married couple could not be traced to the interview.
155907.g: Won Best Original Anime at the 8th Crunchyroll Anime Awards (2024). It's about two men raised in violence learning to raise a child gently, found family over blood, and breaking an abusive family line, which Rei does literally by giving up the arm his father trained to kill.

21202.meta: 2016 · Studio Deen · TV, 10 episodes (season 1) · light novels by Natsume Akatsuki (2013–2020, 17 volumes)
21202.w: Kazuma Satou, a teenage shut-in, dies a pointless death saving a girl from a tractor he thinks is a truck. In the afterlife, the goddess Aqua offers him rebirth in a game-like fantasy world with one bonus item or power, and out of spite he picks Aqua herself, dragging her down with him to the starter town of Axel. Broke, they do day labor instead of adventuring and build a hopeless party: Megumin, an archmage who can cast one huge explosion a day, and Darkness, a noble crusader who can't land a hit and wants to be hurt. The season parodies isekai and RPG tropes. Ending: the giant walking fortress Destroyer heads for Axel, the town and the party destroy it, Kazuma teleports its exploding core away, it lands on a noble's mansion, and Kazuma is arrested.
21202.q: ⚠ No LGBTQ+ content found in season 1 and no critical discussion of it as LGBTQ+ media. Its sexual humor (Darkness's masochism, Kazuma's panty-stealing skill) is what comes up in forums.
21202.g: The best-known parody of the isekai boom: a "chosen hero" who is petty and lazy, with a party of useless misfits. Critics praised the comedy, voice acting and music. It placed 10th among TV anime in Newtype's 2015–16 awards and won "Isekai Series of the Decade" in Funimation's 2019 poll, and went on to more seasons, films and spin-offs.

137822.meta: 2022–23 · Eight Bit · TV, 24 episodes (season 1) · manga by Muneyuki Kaneshiro and Yusuke Nomura (2018–)
137822.w: After Japan finishes 16th at the 2018 World Cup, the Japan Football Association hires the eccentric coach Jinpachi Ego to run "Blue Lock," a sealed facility where 300 high-school forwards compete to become the world's most selfish, ego-driven striker; losers are barred from the national team for good. Yoichi Isagi, a team player who just missed a big shot, lands on Team Z, the lowest-ranked group, with Meguru Bachira, a dribbler who talks about the "monster" inside him, Kunigami and the sprinter Chigiri. Others include the lazy genius Nagi and his partner Reo, the arrogant Barou and top-ranked Rin Itoshi. Team Z climbs from last to advance; in the second selection players "steal" each other after wins. Ending: Rin's team takes Isagi, then loses 1–5 to five world-class pros. Ego saves the program with a counter-proposal: a match against Japan's U-20 team, including Rin's brother Sae, with the national-team spots on the line.
137822.q: ⚠ No confirmed LGBTQ+ character in the anime. Its queer life is in the fandom, which is large: Archive of Our Own lists 2,706 works tagged Bachira/Isagi, and fans read its mutually obsessive rivalries (Isagi/Bachira, Nagi/Reo) as charged. One article notes that sports anime are often queer-coded without being queer representation. The character fans most often call gay is Shidou, for flirting with Sae Itoshi; the author has never confirmed it, and ⚠ that material is mostly from later manga chapters (Shidou appears only in season 1's final episode).
137822.g: It flips the sports-anime formula: instead of teamwork, it argues that selfishness and ego make a great striker, which split viewers. The manga won the 45th Kodansha Manga Award (2021) and has 65M+ copies in circulation. The anime won the New Face Award at the 2023 Japan Character Awards. ANN called it "a really good time" for fans of camp; IGN called it "a fairly typical sports anime."

124153.meta: 2021 · Bones · TV, 12 episodes (+ Extra Part OVA, 2025) · original, created and directed by Hiroko Utsumi
124153.w: Present-day Okinawa, where an underground midnight skateboard race called "S" runs down an abandoned mine; skaters settle "beefs" with one-on-one races, with betting on the side. Reki Kyan, a high-school skater who builds his own boards, brings Langa Hasegawa, a half-Japanese transfer student from Canada, into S. Langa has never skated but grew up snowboarding, and he improves so fast that he becomes Reki's rival as well as his best friend, which opens a painful rift before they make up. The adult regulars keep day jobs: Cherry Blossom (Kaoru), a calligrapher who skates with an AI board; Joe (Kojiro), who runs an Italian restaurant and is Cherry's bickering childhood friend; Shadow, a florist; and Miya, a junior-high prodigy. The antagonist is Adam (Ainosuke Shindo), S's founder and a politician, raised to treat abuse as love, who wants Langa as his "Eve." Ending: Langa races Adam on S's original course, loses himself until he sees the word "fun" Reki wrote on his board, and wins. Adam finds his own joy in skating again, and Reki and Langa race each other as promised, echoing episode 1. ⚠ Who wins that final race isn't confirmed; a second season was announced in 2022.
124153.q: The show never states that Reki and Langa are together, but their partnership is its emotional center, and reviewers read it as close friendship or something more. The Geekiary's reviewer said the ambiguity "never feels like queerbaiting." Adam is the most clearly queer-coded character, "more explicitly implied to be gay," which makes him a live debate: a gay-coded villain whose cruelty comes from an abusive upbringing reads to some as a real picture of queer damage and to others as the old predatory-queer-villain trope. Cherry and Joe are the other big fan pairing. Director Hiroko Utsumi also directed Free! and Banana Fish, both central to queer anime fandom. ⚠ A forum claim that Adam proposes to Tadashi in the finale is unconfirmed.
124153.g: A sports anime about why you play: the finale turns on remembering that skating is supposed to be fun, against Adam's "poisoned" love of the sport. Langa's grief for his dead father and Reki's fear of being left behind by a more talented friend give the races real stakes, and its adult cast with day jobs is unusual for the genre. Anime Feminist's premiere review objected to early misogynist jokes and the near-absence of female racers.

227.meta: 2000 · Gainax / Production I.G · OVA, 6 episodes · original, directed by Kazuya Tsurumaki, written by Yōji Enokido, music by The Pillows
227.w: Mabase, a sleepy suburb dominated by a factory shaped like a giant clothes iron. It belongs to Medical Mechanica, a corporation whose goal is to press the wrinkles out of the brain. Naota, 12, works hard at seeming adult and insists nothing amazing ever happens in Mabase. His older brother is playing baseball in the US, and the brother's ex-girlfriend Mamimi clings to Naota. Then Haruko Haruhara runs him over on a Vespa and hits him on the head with a bass guitar, opening a portal in his forehead that robots come out of. Haruko moves in as the family's maid, claiming to be a Galactic Space Police investigator; she's really chasing Atomsk, a space-bending being Medical Mechanica holds captive. The first robot out of Naota's head becomes Canti, which Naota merges with to fight. Ending: Medical Mechanica turns its factory into a doomsday device; Naota becomes Atomsk's host, defeats the threat and releases Atomsk into space. Haruko chases Atomsk and leaves Naota behind; per a staff interview, he tells her he loves her and she calls him "just a kid." Sequel seasons followed in 2018 and 2023.
227.q: ⚠ No queer reading found in a source, and no LGBTQ+ characters in the OVA. /Film says the show refuses to hide adolescent sexuality behind "cutesy, chaste tropes," and the horn that grows from Naota's head near a crush is a running puberty metaphor. One forum reader asks whether Naota wants to be with Haruko or wants to be her. ⚠ A scene where Haruko and Mamimi tease him by pretending to be lesbians is in the manga, not the anime.
227.g: One of the anime that taught a US audience what the medium could do: it premiered on Adult Swim in 2003 and built a cult following. Tsurumaki set out to "break the rules," cutting it like a music video, and said "comprehension should not be an important factor." It won Best Comedy and Best Short Series at the 2007 American Anime Awards. The Avatar: The Last Airbender staff were told to watch every episode, and Tatsuki Fujimoto called Chainsaw Man a "wicked version of FLCL." Underneath the chaos is a kid learning to set boundaries with adults who use him.

98436.meta: 2017–18 · Wit Studio · TV, 24 episodes (season 2, 2023) · manga by Kore Yamazaki
98436.w: Modern Britain, where a hidden world of magic sits beside ordinary life: fae, dragons, church grims and silkies are real but invisible to most people. Chise Hatori is an orphaned Japanese teenager whose father left and whose mother killed herself in front of her. Unwanted by her relatives, she sells herself at an auction in London, and Elias Ainsworth buys her for five million pounds: a seven-foot magus with an animal skull for a head, part fae and part human, with no memory of where he came from. He tells her she is a Sleigh Beggy, someone who draws in magic so strongly it will kill her within a few years, makes her his apprentice, and announces she will be his bride. The household includes Ruth, a church-grim dog who becomes her familiar and brother figure, and Silver, a silkie housekeeper. The antagonist is Cartaphilus, the immortal "Wandering Jew" whose body rots forever. Chise absorbs a dying dragon's curse that twists her arm, and Cartaphilus swaps it for his own. Ending: Chise sings Cartaphilus into rest instead of destroying him, and she and Elias promise to stay together in a mock wedding with rings and vows.
98436.q: ⚠ No source found on LGBTQ+ characters or a queer reading; its central romance is Chise and Elias. What it does have is found family: abandoned people, a monster and fae spirits building a home that has nothing to do with blood. It opens with a teenager being bought, and the age gap and ownership are a long-running criticism of the premise.
98436.g: It takes depression, suicide and abandonment seriously: Chise starts with "nothing to live for," and one reviewer notes that "loss, depression, grief, abandonment, and pain are all explored," each turning toward healing. Elias is the other half, a being never taught to be human, learning empathy. It draws on British and Irish folklore (leanan sídhe, church grims, silkies, changelings) more carefully than most fantasy anime.

14513.meta: 2012–13 · A-1 Pictures · TV, 25 episodes (season 2, 2013–14) · manga by Shinobu Ohtaka (2009–2017, 37 volumes)
14513.w: A fantasy world built from One Thousand and One Nights: desert kingdoms, slave markets, sea trade and rival empires. "Dungeons" have risen across the land, and whoever conquers one becomes master of a djinn and its "metal vessel." Fate is carried by the "Rukh," birdlike spirits of life, and rare magicians called Magi choose kings. Aladdin, a cheerful boy who spent his life sealed in a room with the djinn Ugo in his flute, discovers he is a Magi. He befriends Alibaba, a broke young man who dreams of dungeon riches, and they conquer the dungeon Amon together. They free Morgiana, a slave from the Fanalis warrior people, and meet Sinbad, king of Sindria and a legendary dungeon conqueror. Alibaba turns out to be the exiled prince of Balbadd and leads a revolt against his corrupt brother, while the Kou Empire swallows the country. Behind it all is Al-Thamen, a secret group pulling people into "depravity," with the magi Judar as its face. Ending: in the dungeon Zagan, Hakuryuu of Kou loses an arm protecting Alibaba, Alibaba is dragged into depravity and Aladdin pulls him back, and Zagan chooses Hakuryuu as its master. ⚠ Finale details from one source.
14513.q: ⚠ No source found on LGBTQ+ characters or queer readings. Fanlore lists fan pairings such as Sinbad/Ja'far and Judar/Hakuryuu, which are fandom, not canon.
14513.g: A big shōnen adventure that is really about politics: who deserves to rule, what slavery and debt do to people, and whether fate can be refused. Morgiana's arc is about choosing freedom after enslavement; Alibaba's is about a failed prince trying to deserve his people. The manga won the 59th Shogakukan Manga Award (2014) and had 25M+ copies in circulation by 2018.

21709.meta: 2016 · MAPPA · TV, 12 episodes · original by director Sayo Yamamoto and writer Mitsurō Kubo
21709.w: The real world of men's figure skating: the Grand Prix series, short and free programs, scores and exhibitions. Yuri Katsuki, 23 and Japan's top skater, has anxiety. After a disastrous Grand Prix Final he goes home to Hasetsu (based on Karatsu, Saga), ready to quit. A video of him skating his idol Victor Nikiforov's routine goes viral, and Victor, the five-time world champion, shows up at the family's hot-spring inn offering to coach him. Fifteen-year-old Russian prodigy Yuri Plisetsky comes to claim Victor's promise to coach him instead; Victor sets the two Yuris against each other with two arrangements of one melody, agape and eros. Yuri Katsuki wins, and the season follows coach and skater growing closer through the Grand Prix. Ending: in Barcelona, Yuri buys matching gold rings and he and Victor exchange them. At the Final, Yuri breaks Victor's free-skate world record but Plisetsky narrowly takes gold. Victor wants to compete again, Yuri asks him to stay on as coach, and Yuri moves to St. Petersburg to train with him; they skate "Stay Close to Me" together in the exhibition. The sequel film was cancelled in 2024.
21709.q: A mainstream TV sports anime in which two men fall in love and exchange rings. Critics called that unusual for anime, in a country that doesn't recognize same-sex marriage and a sport with its own homophobia problems. The episode 7 kiss is hidden behind Victor's arms; the director reportedly faced censorship over the scene, and the framing left some viewers arguing whether it happened. Some critics praised it for treating the relationship as an adult romance outside the yaoi genre, with characters whose arcs aren't only about their sexuality; others called a world with no homophobia at all unrealistic. For many viewers it was a landmark: one Out Write essayist writes about breaking down after the episode 7 kiss.
21709.g: It portrays anxiety honestly, through Yuri's inner monologue and how he skates through panic. Real skaters, including Johnny Weir and Adam Rippon, praised it, and two skaters performed to its music at the 2018 Winter Olympics. It won all seven categories it was nominated for at the first Crunchyroll Anime Awards, including Anime of the Year, and Animation of the Year (TV) at the Tokyo Anime Award Festival. It brought about 20,000 visitors from 27 countries to Karatsu by May 2017.

177697.meta: 2024 · Production +h · ONA, 18 episodes (also a two-part film) · manga by Inio Asano (2014–2022, 12 volumes)
177697.w: A huge alien mothership has hung motionless over Tokyo since "8/31," three years before the story starts, and it never quite attacks. The military keeps shooting down small "invaders" with US-supplied weapons, and the public argues online over whether the aliens are a threat or the real victims. Daily life goes on underneath, and that's the real subject. The leads are two high-school best friends: Kadode Koyama, an anxious manga fan whose father went missing on 8/31, and Ouran "Ontan" Nakagawa, a loud, chaotic girl who calls their bond "absolute." Around them are their friend group (Kiho, Rin, Ai) and later university friends, plus Keita Ōba, a teen idol possessed by an invader. The city slowly decays as they grow up, and the ship starts to break apart. A time-travel twist reveals Ontan came from an earlier timeline where Kadode died, and Ontan used an alien device to save her; the world of the series is the cost. Ending: the last episodes show several timelines side by side: the original, where the friendship broke and Kadode died; the main one, ending in catastrophe; and one with no invasion, where the two stay friends into old age. ⚠ The anime's final episodes are confirmed only by a contradictory fan summary.
177697.q: The whole emotional structure is a love between two girls that outranks everything, the world included: Ontan rewrites reality for Kadode, knowing it may doom humanity, because losing her is the worst outcome she can imagine. Reviewers call the friendship "absolute," and one manga review argues Asano seems to want to make them a couple but "can't bring himself to do it." It never becomes explicitly romantic. ⚠ Wikipedia describes a character who moved to Tokyo to escape small-town gender norms and dresses in women's clothing among accepting friends; not confirmed elsewhere. Rin is a fan of boys' love manga.
177697.g: Asano uses an alien invasion to show how people normalize disaster: everyone keeps scrolling, studying and joking while the government lies and the sky rots, read as a portrait of post-Fukushima Japan and extremely online politics. The manga won the 66th Shogakukan Manga Award (2021) and a Japan Media Arts Festival Excellence Award (2022), was nominated for an Eisner (2019), and has 3M+ copies in circulation.

163270.meta: 2024 · CloverWorks · TV, 13 episodes (season 2, 2025) · web manga by Satoru Nii (2021–)
163270.w: Furin High School in the town of Makochi has the lowest grades and the toughest fighters. It used to be a school of brawling delinquents, but its students have become "Bofurin," a gang that protects the town's shopkeepers and residents instead of terrorizing them. Haruka Sakura, a lone fighter with heterochromia who has been rejected his whole life, shows up wanting only to climb to the top, and finds a town that thanks him. His class includes Nirei, a weak fighter who takes notes on everyone, the calm, teasing Suō, and his silent rival Sugishita. Above them are the third-year leader Umemiya and the "Four Kings," and Kotoha, who runs a café, is Sakura's first friend in town. The main arc is a rule-bound showdown with the rival gang Shishitoren, through which Sakura learns what fighting for other people means. Ending: Sakura is made grade captain and reaches out first to help a classmate who keeps turning up bruised and lying about it, setting up season 2.
163270.q: Tasuku "Tsubaki-chan" Tsubakino, one of the Four Kings, is among the most-discussed queer characters in recent shōnen. He identifies as male, wears women's fashion and makeup, fights in heels, is a pole dancer, and has an openly acknowledged, unreturned crush on another Bofurin member, and the gang treats all of it as simply who he is. Mihaela Mihailova (In Media Res, 2025) argues the show redefines delinquent-genre masculinity: strength from self-acceptance, empathy and emotional honesty, the brotherhood as a safe space that respects difference. Critics note he isn't a punchline, a token or queerbait, and the English dub cast a queer actor of color, Kiba Walker. ⚠ His main arc is in season 2; sources disagree on his pronouns.
163270.g: It takes the delinquent-fight genre (Tokyo Revengers, Crows) and changes its purpose from dominance to protection and community, with a damaged, isolated lead learning to accept being cared for. CloverWorks' fight animation earned a Best Action nomination at the 2025 Crunchyroll Anime Awards. The manga has passed 10M copies, and a live-action film followed in 2025.

98659.meta: 2017 · Lerche · TV, 12 episodes (later seasons 2022, 2024, 2026) · light novel by Shōgo Kinugasa (2015–)
98659.w: The Advanced Nurturing High School is a government-run elite school that looks like paradise: students get 100,000 points a month (1 point = 1 yen) to spend on campus. The catch is that classes are ranked A to D, points depend on each class's collective behavior and exam results, and a failing student is expelled. Kiyotaka Ayanokōji, quiet and seemingly bland, is placed in Class D, the class for "defective" students, with the cold, proud Suzune Horikita and the relentlessly nice Kikyō Kushida, who hides a two-faced personality. Without anyone noticing, he engineers the class's survival, including clearing classmate Sudō of an assault complaint set up by Class C. Ending: the class trip turns into a week-long survival exam on a deserted island. Class D wins after Ayanokōji secretly makes himself leader and wrecks every other class's guesses. He reveals his father is trying to get him expelled, and admits in voice-over that he sees his classmates as tools to use, as long as he wins.
98659.q: ⚠ No source found on LGBTQ+ characters or themes in season 1. Several characters (Kushida, Karuizawa, Sakura) survive by hiding their real selves behind an acceptable mask, inside an institution that sorts people into worthy and defective.
98659.g: A cold satire of meritocracy and Japan's exam-ranking culture: the school preaches freedom while quietly scoring everyone, and the hero wins by treating people as pieces. The light novels have sold 10.8M+ copies, among the best-selling of all time.

151801.meta: 2023 · A-1 Pictures · TV, 12 episodes (season 2, 2024) · manga by Hajime Kōmoto (2020–2023, 18 volumes)
151801.w: Everyone uses magic for everything, and a person's magic level decides their social rank. People born without magic are treated as defective and, by law, hunted down and executed. Mash Burnedead, raised in secret in the forest by his adoptive father Regro, has no magic at all, just absurd strength from relentless training and a deadpan love of cream puffs. Discovered by the police, he's offered a deal: become a "Divine Visionary," the elite title for Easton Magic Academy's top students, or his father will be punished. Mash fakes his way through spell classes physically, punching spells and outrunning broomsticks, and picks up friends Finn, Lemon, Lance and Dot. The main enemy is Magia Lupus, an elitist student faction led by Abel Walker. Ending: Mash beats Abel, then smashes the mirror of an attacker from the shadowy Innocent Zero with his bare hands, and the whole academy learns he has no magic.
151801.q: ⚠ No source found on LGBTQ+ characters. Its premise is a society that declares one kind of person defective at birth, denies them rights and forces them to hide and "pass" to stay alive. Reason reads it as a metaphor for state discrimination, and a manga review names its theme as "discrimination against those that are different." Mash wins by being exactly who he is instead of learning to blend in.
151801.g: A gag-comedy parody of Harry Potter crossed with One-Punch Man, with pointed jokes about authoritarianism and magical aristocracy. It won Best Comedy at the 2025 Crunchyroll Anime Awards, and the manga has passed 10M copies. Season 2's opening, Creepy Nuts' "Bling-Bang-Bang-Born," became a global viral hit.

159831.meta: 2023 · BUG FILMS · TV, 12 episodes · manga by Haro Aso and Kotaro Takata (2018–)
159831.w: Akira Tendo, 24, has spent three years at a brutally exploitative Tokyo production company: working all night, screamed at by his boss, too drained to ask out his co-worker. When a zombie outbreak hits Tokyo, his first reaction is joy: he never has to go to work again. He writes a list of 100 things to do before he becomes a zombie, rendered in loud neon against the grey of his old life. With him are his old university friend Kencho, a former real-estate agent who wants to be a comedian; Shizuka, a cold, efficient ex-accountant who gradually learns to want things; and later Beatrix, a katana-wielding German Japan-fan. Ending: they reach Akira's home village, threatened by a rival group that unleashes zombies on it. The zombies are sealed in a tunnel, Akira's father turns out to be alive, and the group sets off to keep chasing their dreams.
159831.q: ⚠ No source found on LGBTQ+ characters; its romances are straight. It's about someone who survived years in a place that crushed him finally breaking free and choosing his own life, with a found family instead of the obligations he was given.
159831.g: It turns the zombie apocalypse into a story of liberation and a direct satire of Japan's overwork culture: the apocalypse is less frightening than the office. Critics compared Akira's outlook to how people rethought work during COVID. The manga earned two Eisner nominations (2022); the anime got six Crunchyroll Anime Awards nominations and was selected for Annecy 2024. IGN noted animation problems from production delays.

151806.meta: 2023 · Lay-duce · TV, 13 episodes · four-panel manga by Fumita Yanagida (2015–2019, 8 volumes)
151806.w: A present-day high-school comedy with no fantasy. Tomo Aizawa is a tomboy who is very good at combat sports (her father runs a karate dojo) and is in love with her childhood friend and neighbor Jun Kubota, who treats her as "one of the boys." Around them are Misuzu, Tomo's sharp, teasing best friend, who is wary of losing Tomo to Jun, and Carol, a wealthy British-descended school idol who starts as Tomo's rival and becomes her friend. It's episodic slapstick: Tomo keeps trying to make Jun see her as a girl, and her friends help and hinder in about equal measure. Her first confession lands her in the friend zone, because Jun sees her as a buddy, not because he has no feelings for her. Ending: Jun challenges Tomo's father for permission to date her and wins by breaking his nose, then asks Tomo to be his girlfriend, and she accepts with a kiss.
151806.q: It's about gender expression, not sexuality; the romance is straight and no LGBTQ+ character was found in any source. What it gives is a girl who never fits feminine norms and wins the romance anyway. Reviewers read it as showing how "antiquated gender norms get in the way of love," with Tomo's failure to conform as both the comedy and the depth of her character. ⚠ Misuzu's possessive attachment to Tomo invites a queer-coded reading; no source makes it.
151806.g: A tight, complete romcom that adapts the manga to its end and finishes with a real couple, which reviewers called a breath of fresh air after a run of harem shows. The manga won the web manga category of the 2016 Next Manga Award. The Blu-ray review raises the question that gives it weight: is Jun really oblivious, or afraid of what admitting it would change?

323.meta: 2004 · Madhouse · TV, 13 episodes · original, created and directed by Satoshi Kon, music by Susumu Hirasawa
323.w: Present-day Tokyo, where a public panic spreads like a rumor. Tsukiko Sagi, a shy designer who created Maromi, a hugely popular pink dog mascot, is attacked by a boy on golden inline skates with a bent golden bat. Detectives Ikari, tough and skeptical, and Maniwa, drawn to the strangeness of the case, follow a chain of attacks by "Lil' Slugger." Every victim is someone mentally cornered, and the attacker grows stronger the more people talk about him. Many episodes break off to follow one person: a hall-monitor schoolboy, a woman with a second personality, a corrupt cop, a suicide-pact trio, an anime production crew. Lil' Slugger turns out to be something Tsukiko's mind created, and Maromi is the other face of the same escape. Ending: a black mass swallows a ruined Tokyo. As a child, Tsukiko let go of her puppy's leash and it was killed; afraid of her father, she blamed an invented attacker. Once she accepts responsibility, the attacks stop. Two years later the city has recovered, with a hint the cycle could start again.
323.q: Episode 8, "Happy Family Planning," follows three people from an internet suicide pact: an old man, Fuyubachi; a young man, Zebra; and a little girl, Kamome. Zebra is a gay man: a locket holds photos of him with another man, and during a subway suicide attempt he sees a man's spirit walk away. One review ties his despair to being a sexual minority; another critic finds the farcical tone cheapens the suicides. It's a brief, unstated portrait of a closeted gay man's grief in 2004 Japan, told as a dark comedy about three people who keep failing to die and end up caring for each other. ⚠ A Zebra/Fuyubachi romance is fan interpretation, not canon.
323.g: Satoshi Kon's only TV series. Rotten Tomatoes rates it 100%, "a disturbing meditation on individual and societal anxiety," and critics have praised its depiction of depression. It was a Jury Recommended Work at the 8th Japan Media Arts Festival. Its core idea: a society would rather invent a monster than face responsibility, and comforting mascots are part of the same escape.

162804.meta: 2024 · Doga Kobo · TV, 12 episodes · light novel by SunSunSun (2021–)
162804.w: An elite Tokyo high school where the student council election is high-stakes politics. Alisa "Alya" Kujou is half-Russian, aloof, top of her class, and sometimes mutters flirtatious lines in Russian, assuming no one understands. Her seatmate Masachika Kuze, a slacker otaku, understands every word and pretends not to. He was once heir to the powerful Suou family and left after his parents divorced. His younger sister Yuki Suou, now the heiress, is Alya's rival for council president, and Alya's older sister Maria turns out to be Masachika's childhood first love. Masachika agrees to run as Alya's vice-president. Ending: at the term-end ceremony Alya and Yuki formally announce their candidacies, and Alya's speech, after Masachika coaches her through her nerves, draws more applause than Yuki's. The election is left for season 2.
162804.q: ⚠ No LGBTQ+ character or storyline found; the romance is straight. Alya is a half-Russian outsider who can only say what she feels in a second language.
162804.g: A commercial phenomenon: the novels went from 500,000 copies in 2022 to five million by August 2024, and Kadokawa reported about ¥1B in quarterly franchise revenue. It won Slice of Life Anime of the Year at the 11th Anime Trending Awards, and the campaign plot gives it more structure than most romcoms.

98861.meta: 2017– · G.CMay Animation & Film for Tencent · Chinese donghua, 12 episodes (S1) + OVA, film (2019), S2 (2020), S3 (2024) · web novel by Hu Dielan (2011)
98861.w: Present-day China, where a massively popular online game called Glory has a professional esports league. Ye Xiu, a founding legend of the pro scene called the "Battle God," is forced out of Team Excellent Era, and his signature character goes to a younger player. He takes a night-shift job at Happy Internet Cafe, owned by Chen Guo, a fan of his. When Glory opens its tenth server, he builds a new character, Lord Grim, from scratch, and keeps breaking the dungeon records the big guilds want. He gathers a new crew: Chen Guo, cafe employee Tang Rou, his longtime partner Su Mucheng and others, against rival pros across the league. Ending: across the seasons, Ye Xiu builds Team Happy and challenges his old team. ⚠ The season 1 finale and the novel's ending are not confirmed in a source.
98861.q: ⚠ No LGBTQ+ content found in canon. ⚠ Its all-male rival roster is known online as a shipping fandom, and Chinese broadcast rules limit same-sex content in official productions; neither is confirmed in a source read here.
98861.g: One of the flagship donghua that showed Chinese studios could make polished action for an international audience. It won Gold for Best Serial Animation at the 14th China Animation Golden Dragon Awards. It treats esports as a real sport with careers, aging out and comebacks: a veteran pushed aside by a commercial machine who rebuilds from zero. A live-action series followed in 2019.

1281.meta: 2000 · Studio Pierrot · TV, 20 episodes · children's books by Tōru Tsunemitsu · English dub by ADV Films (2005)
1281.w: A small Japanese town where development is breaking old seals and letting ghosts loose. Satsuki Miyanoshita moves to her late mother Kayako's hometown with her father and timid younger brother Keiichirou, and finds her mother's diary, a ghost-sealing handbook: Kayako had sealed the ghosts now escaping. With her fearless friend Momoko, reckless neighbor Hajime and the cowardly "paranormal expert" Leo, she exorcises a ghost almost every episode, often in the abandoned old school building. Early on she accidentally seals the demon Amanojaku inside her cat Kaya, and he slowly becomes a grudging helper. Ending: to buy Satsuki time to seal the strongest ghost, Lord Ōma, with the old school's bell, Amanojaku leaves the cat and fights him, sacrificing himself. Ōma is sealed with Amanojaku, and the diary goes blank.
1281.q: Nothing queer in the Japanese original; the English dub is the story. ADV had loose orders (keep the names, how each ghost is beaten, and each episode's core plot), so it rewrote the show as an improvised, politically incorrect comedy. In the dub, Satsuki's mother is described as bisexual or lesbian and a teacher is implied to be a cross-dresser, alongside jokes about abortion, abuse, disability and religion. Queer identities appear only as punchlines, which makes the dub a document of mid-2000s American humor about queerness more than representation.
1281.g: The dub is one of the most famous in anime history: written by Steven Foster and Lucan Duran, with cast members like Greg Ayres and Monica Rial ad-libbing. It was booed at its Otakon 2005 premiere, then won Anime Insider's 2006 Dub of the Year over Fullmetal Alchemist, and is credited as a forerunner of abridged and parody dubs. The story that the show flopped in Japan is a myth: it peaked at an 11.8% rating, sometimes beating Pokémon. Discotek's 2014 release has both versions side by side.

6024.meta: 2009 · Madhouse · TV shorts, 104 episodes × 3 min (season 2) · manga by Kanata Konami (2004–2015, 12 volumes)
6024.w: An ordinary Japanese city seen mostly at a kitten's eye level. Chi, a small grey-and-white kitten separated from her mother, was taken in by the Yamada family: father, mother and toddler son Yohei. Their apartment building bans pets, so they've been hiding her, and this season they decide it's unfair to keep her hidden and plan to find her another home. Each 3-minute episode is a small adventure built on cat logic and the family's efforts to keep her secret, plus run-ins with a big black cat who acts as her rough mentor. Ending: the Yamadas can't give Chi up and move to a house where pets are allowed. Chi gets lost, meets the black cat again and finds her way back, and the final episode, "Chi Makes a Family," ends with a party for her.
6024.q: ⚠ No source discusses LGBTQ+ content; there are no queer characters or storylines. Chi loses her birth family and is claimed by people who aren't her kin, and the family hides her from a building that forbids her existence, then moves rather than give her up.
6024.g: The manga ran eleven years in full color, and Vertical's English edition was one of the better-known all-ages manga in North America. The comedy comes from closely observed kitten behavior instead of plot, and it's a widely cited example of gentle iyashikei ("healing") anime for children.

20920.meta: 2015 · J.C.Staff · TV, 13 episodes · light novels by Fujino Ōmori
20920.w: The city of Orario sits on top of the Dungeon, a huge labyrinth that keeps producing monsters. Gods have come down to the mortal world, each leading a "Familia" whose members gain RPG-style stats and levels through their god's blessing. Bell Cranel is a naive rookie and the only member of the Familia of Hestia, a small, poor goddess who adores him. His grandfather told him the Dungeon is a place to meet girls; instead, the swordswoman Ais Wallenstein keeps rescuing him, he falls for her, and his rare skill makes him grow fast out of longing to catch up. The cast grows to include Lili, Welf and Ryuu, plus scheming gods like Freya and Hermes. Ending: stranded on Floor 18, the adventurers pool their attacks against an enhanced Goliath so Bell can land the final blow, and the season closes with a celebration back in Orario.
20920.q: ⚠ Light, from fan sources only. The goddess Loki, who leads Ais's Familia, is drawn as tomboyish and played for comedy as openly interested in women, flirting with the women in her Familia, especially Ais. No critic treats it as representation. The show itself is a straight harem premise with fan service, so the queer content is a side gag.
20920.g: One of the biggest light-novel franchises of the 2010s, with several seasons, a spin-off and films. ⚠ Hestia's blue "ribbon" became a viral fan-art craze in 2015. Under the harem title, it's an earnest growth story about an underdog who refuses to stay rescued.

100977.meta: 2018 · David Production · TV, 13 episodes + special · manga by Akane Shimizu (2015–2021)
100977.w: The inside of a human body drawn as a busy city, with each type of cell as a uniformed worker. Red blood cells are couriers carrying oxygen through streets of blood vessels; white blood cells (neutrophils) are white-clad killers who hunt germs on sight; Killer T cells are a muscle-bound strike squad; macrophages are smiling maids with giant weapons; platelets are small children who patch wounds. The lead is AE3803, a clumsy rookie red blood cell who keeps getting lost, and U-1146, a neutrophil brutal in combat and gentle outside it, who keeps running into her. Each episode is a real medical event: a scrape, flu, food poisoning, allergy, cancer cells, heatstroke. Ending: in "Hemorrhagic Shock," a head injury drains the body's blood; AE3803 refuses to stop working while a cynical trainee says it's pointless, a transfusion arrives, and the body recovers.
100977.q: ⚠ No source discusses a queer reading. Every cell type is given a gender for its character design even though cells have none, and the body is drawn as a diverse workforce of very different people keeping the whole alive. Its romance is the bashful pull between U-1146 and AE3803.
100977.g: One of the most successful educational anime ever made: biology teachers in China assigned it as homework for its accuracy, and an Emory medical-school researcher praised its depiction of cancer cells. It turns immunology into memorable action, and led to a second season and the darker spin-off CODE BLACK.

106479.meta: 2020 · Silver Link · TV, 12 episodes (season 2, 2023) · light novel by Yuumikan
106479.w: High schooler Kaede Honjou joins the VR game NewWorld Online because her best friend Risa invited her. Her avatar is Maple, and because she hates pain she puts every point into defense: slow, no magic, but impossible to hurt. Her odd thinking and luck stack absurd skills: she eats a poison hydra and gains its poison, earns "Absolute Defense," and later gets a mechanical form and a monster form, becoming a game-breaking celebrity the developers keep patching around. Risa joins as Sally, an agile evasion fighter and the pair's tactician, and they build a guild, Maple Tree. Ending: in the guild war Maple beats the rival guild leaders, Maple Tree finishes third, the admins leave her alone because she brought in so many players, and she invites the rival guilds to watch the highlights together.
106479.q: The heart of the show is Maple and Sally: Sally brings Maple into the game, plans every fight around her, and wants above all to be the one who can stand next to her. Fans and some reviewers read them as yuri; Anime News Network's season 2 review describes a "married couple" dynamic and calls Maple Sally's "GF," and a light-novel reviewer says later volumes lean into romantic subtext that stays deniable. The cast is almost all girls, with no boyfriend storyline. ⚠ Officially presented as friendship.
106479.g: A well-known parody of the gamer-isekai genre: instead of a grim power fantasy, its overpowered hero is a cheerful girl who breaks the meta by doing what's fun. The web novel passed 60M views.

114121.meta: 2020 · Haoliners Animation League · Chinese donghua, 15 episodes × ~18 min (S1) · web novel by Kuxuan (2017)
114121.w: A modern China where cultivation, the Daoist-fantasy practice of building spiritual power, is as ordinary as school sports. Wang Ling has advanced a realm every two years since infancy; at sixteen his power could destroy the world, so his parents seal it, and his emotions with it, in a talisman that is slowly wearing out. All he wants is a quiet life at school.
